title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 2
paragraphs: Napoleon left Dresden on the twenty-ninth of May, after three weeks there among a court of princes, dukes, kings, and even an emperor. Before he went, he rewarded the emperor, kings, and princes who deserved it and scolded those he was unhappy with. To the Empress of Austria he gave pearls and diamonds that were his own — that is, ones he had taken from other kings. And, as his historian tells us, he embraced the Empress Marie Louise tenderly. She regarded him as her husband, though he had left another wife in Paris, and she was left grieving by the parting, which she seemed hardly able to bear. The diplomats still firmly believed peace was possible and worked zealously for it, and Napoleon himself wrote Alexander a letter, addressing him as Monsieur mon frère and sincerely assuring him that he did not want war and would always love and honor him. Even so, he set off to join his army, and at every station he issued fresh orders to hurry his troops along from west to east. He rode in a coach and six, with pages, aides-de-camp, and an escort around him, on the road through Posen, Thorn, Danzig, and Königsberg. In every one of these towns, thousands of people greeted him with excitement and enthusiasm.

The army was moving from west to east, and relays of six horses took him the same way. On the tenth of June, * he caught up with the army and spent the night in rooms made ready for him on the estate of a Polish count, in the Vilkavisski forest.
The next day he overtook the army and drove in a carriage to the Niemen. There he changed into a Polish uniform and went down to the riverbank to pick a place for the crossing.

Across the river he saw some Cossacks (les Cosaques) and the wide steppes, with the holy city of Moscow (Moscou, la ville sainte) lying in the midst of them, the capital of a realm like the Scythia that Alexander the Great had marched into. Suddenly, against every strategic and diplomatic consideration, Napoleon ordered the advance, and the next day his army began crossing the Niemen.

Early on the morning of the twelfth of June he stepped out of his tent, pitched that day on the steep left bank of the Niemen, and watched through a spyglass as his troops streamed out of the Vilkavisski forest and poured across the three bridges built over the river. The troops knew the Emperor was there and were looking for him. When they spotted a figure in an overcoat and cocked hat, standing in front of his tent on the hill apart from his suite, they threw their caps in the air and shouted, "Vive l'Empereur!" Regiment after regiment came out in an endless stream from the huge forest that had hidden them, then split apart and flowed on and on across the three bridges to the other side.

"Now we'll go into action. Oh, when he takes it in hand himself, things get hot... by heaven!... There he is!... Vive l'Empereur! So these are the steppes of Asia! It's a nasty country all the same. Au revoir, Beauché; I'll keep the best palace in Moscow for you! Au revoir. Good luck!... Did you see the Emperor? Vive l'Empereur!... preur!—If they make me Governor of India, Gérard, I'll make you Minister of Kashmir — that's settled. Vive l'Empereur! Hurrah! hurrah! hurrah! The Cossacks — those rascals — see how they run! Vive l'Empereur! There he is, do you see him? I've seen him twice, as I see you now. The little corporal... I saw him give the cross to one of the veterans.... Vive l'Empereur!" So called the voices of men young and old, of every sort of character and social standing. Every face wore the same look: joy that the long-awaited campaign was beginning, and rapture and devotion toward the man in the gray coat on the hill.

On the thirteenth of June they brought Napoleon a rather small, thoroughbred Arab horse. He mounted and galloped to one of the bridges over the Niemen. The rapturous cheering never stopped and deafened him. Evidently he put up with it only because he couldn't forbid the soldiers to show their love by shouting, but it followed him everywhere, it disturbed him, and it pulled him away from the military concerns that had occupied him since he joined the army. He crossed one of the swaying pontoon bridges to the far side, turned sharply left, and galloped toward Kovno. Mounted chasseurs of the Guard rode ahead of him, breathless with delight and enraptured, clearing a path for him through the troops. At the broad river Viliya he stopped beside a regiment of Polish Uhlans posted on the bank.
"Vivat!" cried the Poles in ecstasy, breaking ranks and jostling one another to see him.

Napoleon looked up and down the river, got off his horse, and sat on a log lying on the bank. He made a silent sign and someone handed him a telescope. He rested it on the back of a happy page who had run up, and gazed at the opposite bank. Then he bent over a map spread on the logs. Without raising his head he said something, and two of his aides-de-camp galloped off toward the Polish Uhlans.
"What? What did he say?" was heard in the ranks of the Polish Uhlans as one of the aides-de-camp rode up.

The order was to find a ford and cross the river. The colonel of the Polish Uhlans, a handsome old man, turned red and, tripping over his words in his excitement, asked the aide-de-camp if he might swim the river with his Uhlans instead of looking for a ford. He was obviously afraid of being refused, like a boy asking leave to mount a horse, and he begged to be allowed to swim across before the Emperor's eyes. The aide-de-camp answered that the Emperor would probably not be displeased by such excess of zeal.

Hardly had the aide-de-camp said this when the old mustached officer, his face happy and his eyes sparkling, raised his saber and shouted "Vivat!" He ordered the Uhlans to follow, spurred his horse, and galloped into the river. His horse had grown restive under him, and he thrust at it angrily and plunged into the water, heading for the deepest place, where the current ran fast. Hundreds of Uhlans galloped in behind him. Out in the middle of the stream, in the rushing current, it was cold and eerie, and the Uhlans clutched at one another as they fell from their horses. Some horses drowned, and some men. The rest tried to swim on, some still in the saddle, some hanging onto their horses' manes. They struggled toward the opposite bank, and though there was a ford a third of a mile away, they were proud to be swimming and drowning in this river under the eyes of the man sitting on the log, who wasn't even looking at what they were doing. The aide-de-camp came back and, picking a good moment, ventured to point out to the Emperor how devoted the Poles were to him. The little man in the gray overcoat stood up, called Berthier, and began pacing the bank with him, giving him instructions and now and then glancing with disapproval at the drowning Uhlans, who were distracting him.

It was nothing new to him to believe that his presence anywhere in the world, from Africa to the steppes of Muscovy alike, was enough to stun people and drive them to mad self-forgetfulness. He called for his horse and rode back to his quarters.

About forty Uhlans drowned in the river, although boats were sent to help them. Most struggled back to the bank they had left. The colonel and some of his men reached the far side and clambered out with difficulty. And as soon as they were out, in their soaked, streaming clothes, they shouted "Vivat!" and looked ecstatically at the place where Napoleon had been, though he was no longer there, and at that moment thought themselves happy.

That evening Napoleon gave one order that the forged Russian paper money, prepared for use in Russia, should be delivered as quickly as possible, and another that a Saxon should be shot, in whose possession a letter had been found with information about the orders to the French army. Between the two, he also gave instructions that the Polish colonel who had plunged into the river for no reason should be enrolled in the Légion d'honneur, of which Napoleon himself was the head.
* Those whom (God) wishes to destroy he drives mad.
